Chapter 7: Navigating Differences—Finding Common Ground in Unexpected Places.
When you start making new connections, there’s another challenge that pops up—figuring out how to handle all the differences between people.
Think about it: the folks you meet in fresh circles often come from all kinds of backgrounds. They might have beliefs, habits, or histories that don’t look anything like yours. At first, those differences can feel like roadblocks, little reminders that there’s an “us” and a “them.”
But what if, instead of backing away, you leaned in? What if those differences could actually make your world richer?
Picture this—a retired nurse, used to the routines and pecking order of hospital life, decides to join a local writing group. She walks in and finds herself surrounded by everyone from college students to folks in their eighties, each with their own writing style and perspective. At first, she doesn’t quite fit in. Her stories seem a bit old-fashioned, and some people dismiss them.
But instead of shutting down, she listens. She starts to appreciate the others’ experiences. When she shares her own stories, she offers them as glimpses into another time, not lectures. And something shifts. The group begins to learn from each other.
Their differences? They turn into fuel for creativity and inspiration, instead of reasons to stay apart.
Or take the man who’s grown up in a small, tight-knit town. Moving to a bustling city is a shock—so many languages, customs, even the food is unfamiliar. He feels lost in the crowd, unsure how—or even if—he’ll fit in.
Then, one day in the park, someone invites him to join a pick-up soccer game. Suddenly, all the differences melt away. The rules of soccer are the same everywhere, and soon, laughter bridges the gap. Over time, he realizes that shared activities—whether it’s sports, music, or volunteering—can create spaces where differences fade and genuine connection grows.
Most of us have an idea in our heads about who’ll make a good friend, or who’ll “fit” into our lives. It’s natural to look for people who seem similar to us. But honestly? Some of the deepest, most meaningful connections come from the most unexpected places—from people whose stories challenge us and help us grow.
Here’s something to remember: Finding common ground doesn’t mean pretending our differences don’t exist. It’s about being open—willing to listen, to ask questions, and to share honestly. It’s about curiosity, not judgment. It’s about seeing the person, not just the label.
Sure, it can feel awkward at first. But opening yourself up to someone different is incredibly rewarding.
As your circles expand, so does your capacity for empathy and understanding. The world gets bigger, more colorful, and honestly, a whole lot more beautiful.
So, what’s the real takeaway? Belonging isn’t about finding a perfect match. It’s about building bridges—one conversation, one shared moment at a time.
